# Overview {visibility="hidden"}
  



## Open populations
  
Overview

- Population closure is an assumption we make to estimate density in short time periods.
- If we want to study the processes governing spatial {and temporal} variation in density, we need to move  beyond closed population models.
- Open population SCR models allow us to model spatial and temporal variation in survival, recruitment, and movement.
  


## Types of closure
  
Geographic closure
    
- Animals cannot enter or leave the study area
- But what is the study area in non-spatial settings?
- What is a non-spatial setting?
  
Demographic closure
  
- No births or deaths
- Reasonable over short time periods
- But temporal dynamics are often of chief interest
  


## Two varieties of open models
  
Cormack-Jolly-Seber Model
    
- Primarily used to estimate survival
- When permanent emigration is possible, estimate is of "apparent survival" ($\phi$)
- Apparent survival is the probability of surviving and not leaving the study area permanently
- CJS models are not used to estimate abundance or recruitment
  

::: {.fragment}
Jolly-Seber model
  
- Traditionally used to estimate abundance, (apparent) survival, and recruitment
:::
  
  
::: {.fragment}
<center>
Both classes of models can be made spatially explicit to study movement, among other things
</center>
:::




# Non-spatial CJS


## Non-spatial CJS model
  
Notes
    
- Typical scenario involves "releasing" indviduals and recapturing them over time
- We don't model initial capture process
- Instead, we "condition on initial capture"
- As an example, imagine releasing a bunch of tagged animals in a translocation study
- Because we aren't estimating $N$, no data augmentation required
- It is possible to estimate parameters using 1 sampling occasion per season
- Robust design provides more information about $p$
  


## Non-spatial CJS model

State model
$$
    z_{i,t} \sim \mbox{Bernoulli}(z_{i,t-1} \times \phi)
$$
  
Observation model
$$
    y_{i,t} \sim \mbox{Bernoulli}(z_{i,t} \times p)
$$
  
where
  
- $z_{i,t}$ is "alive state" of individual $i$ at time $t$
- $\phi$ is "apparent survival". Probability of being alive and not permanently emigrating. 
- $y_{i,t}=1$ if individual was encountered, $y_{i,t}=0$ otherwise.
  



## Simulating CJS data without robust design

Parameters and dimensions

```{r, echo=-1}
#| label: sim-norobust
set.seed(34918)  
T <- 10               ## primary periods (eg, years)
K <- 1                ## only 1 secondary sampling occasion
n <- 25
phi <- 0.7
p <- 0.4
z <- matrix(NA, n, T)
y <- matrix(NA, n, T)
first <- rpois(n, 1)+1 ## random release dates
```

Generate $z$ and $y$
```{r}
#| label: sim-norbust2
for(i in 1:n) {
    z[i,first[i]] <- 1  ## Known alive at release
    y[i,first[i]] <- 1
    for(t in (first[i]+1):T) {
        z[i,t] <- rbinom(1, 1, z[i,t-1]*phi) ## Alive/dead state
        y[i,t] <- rbinom(1, 1, z[i,t]*p)     ## Data
    }
}
```



## Simulated CJS data

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width='50%'}

Latent alive/dead state
```{r}
#| label: z
z[,1:7]
```
:::
::: {.column width='50%'}


## Likelihood analysis
  
We can fit CJS models in R with the 'RMark' or 'marked' packages. We'll use 'marked', which requires the capture histories to be formatted as a character vector named `ch`. 

```{r}
#| label: marked-data
#| message: false
library(marked)
y.marked <- ifelse(is.na(y), 0, y)
cap.histories <- data.frame(
    ch=apply(y.marked, 1, paste, collapse=""))
head(cap.histories, n=3)
```
  
You can use formulas to model covariate effects.

```{r}
#| label: marked-fit
#| results: 'hide'
#| message: false
fm0 <- crm(data=cap.histories, model="CJS", hessian=TRUE,
           model.parameters=list(Phi=list(formula=~1),
                                 p=list(formula=~1)))
```


## Likelihood analysis

Estimates of apparent survival and capture probability.
```{r}
#| label: marked-predict
predict(fm0)
```

Data

```{r}
#| label: nonsp-data
jags.data.nonsp <- list(y=y, n=n, first=first, T=T)
```
  
Initial values for $z$ matrix
```{r}
#| label: zi
zi.nonsp <- matrix(NA, n, T)
for(i in 1:n) {
    zi.nonsp[i,(first[i]+1):T] <- 1
    }
jags.inits.nonsp <- function() list(phi=runif(1), p=runif(1), z=zi.nonsp)
jags.pars.nonsp <- c("phi", "p")
```
  
Fit the model

```{r}
#| label: jc1

library(jagsUI)
jags.post.samples.nonsp <- jags.basic(data=jags.data.nonsp,

                                      parameters.to.save=jags.pars.nonsp,
                                      model.file="CJS-nonspatial.jag",
                                      n.chains=3, n.adapt=100, n.burnin=0,
                                      n.iter=2000, parallel=TRUE)
```

# Spatial CJS



## Spatial CJS
  
Why spatial?
    
- Comes with all the benefits of other SCR models
- Allows for movement between primary periods, making it possible to separate survival from permanent emigration
- Movement itself may be of interest, such as in studies of dispersal
  
We begin by ignoring movement, but we use the robust design




## Simulating spatial CJS data with robust design

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width='50%'}
Parameters and data dimensions

```{r}
#| label: sim2
T <- 10       # primary occasions
K <- 3        # secondary occasions
n <- 25       # nIndividuals
phi <- 0.7
p0 <- 0.4     # baseline capture prob
sigma <- 0.1  # scale parameter
```

Traps, activity centers, and <br> detection probability
```{r}
#| label: X
co <- seq(0.25, 0.75, length=5)
x <- cbind(rep(co, each=5),
           rep(co, times=5))
J <- nrow(x)
xlim <- ylim <- c(0,1)
s <- cbind(runif(n, xlim[1], xlim[2]),
           runif(n, ylim[1], ylim[2]))
d <- p.sp <- matrix(NA, n, J)
for(i in 1:n) {
    d[i,] <- sqrt((s[i,1]-x[,1])^2 +
                  (s[i,2]-x[,2])^2)
    p.sp[i,] <- p0*exp(-d[i,]^2/(2*sigma^2))
}
```
:::


::: {.column width='50%'}
Generate $z$ and $y$
```{r}
#| label: z2
z <- matrix(NA, n, T)
y.sp <- array(NA, c(n, J, K, T)) ## 4D array
first <- rpois(n, 1)+1 ## random release dates
for(i in 1:n) {
    z[i,first[i]] <- 1
    for(t in (first[i]+1):T) {
        z[i,t] <- rbinom(1, 1,
                         z[i,t-1]*phi)
        for(j in 1:J) {
            y.sp[i,j,1:K,t] <- rbinom(K, 1,
                z[i,t]*p.sp[i,j])
        }
    }
}
```
:::
:::




## Likelihood analysis of spatial CJS model

We'll use the R package 'openpopscr'^[Another option is the
openCR' package.] for model fitting. It isn't on CRAN, but you can install it from github using the following commands.
```{r}
#| label: install-openpopscr
#| message: false
#| results: 'hide'
#| eval: false
library(remotes)
install_github("r-glennie/openpopscr", build = TRUE,
               build_opts = c("--no-resave-data", "--no-manual"),
               build_vignettes = TRUE)
library(openpopscr)
library(secr)
```

If you're on Windows, you might have to install Rtools first.

\url{https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/}



```{r}
#| include: false
library(secr)
library(openpopscr)
```


## Likelihood analysis of spatial CJS model

Begin by making a mask in 'secr'
```{r}
#| label: mask
#| out-width: "60%"
#| fig-align: "center"
trap.df <- data.frame(x*1000); colnames(trap.df) <- c("x","y")
traps <- read.traps(data=trap.df, detector="proximity")
mask <- make.mask(traps=traps, buffer=250)
plot(mask); points(traps, pch=3, col="blue", lwd=2)
```


## Likelihood analysis of spatial CJS model

Format for `secr'
```{r}
#| label: CJS-model-new
y.sp.secr <- y.sp
y.sp.secr[is.na(y.sp)] <- 0
caps <- data.frame(session=1,
                   animal=rep(slice.index(y.sp.secr, 1), y.sp.secr),
                   occasion=rep(slice.index(y.sp.secr, 3:4), y.sp.secr),
                   trap=rep(slice.index(y.sp.secr, 2), y.sp.secr))
capthist <- make.capthist(captures=caps, traps=traps, noccasions=30)
```

Then format for `openpopscr'
```{r}
#| label: format-openpop
cjs.data <- ScrData$new(capthist, mask, primary=rep(1:10, each=3))
```


## Likelihood analysis

Create the model object and then fit it
```{r}
#| label: cjs-mod-fit
#| results: 'hide'
#| cache: true
mod <- CjsModel$new(list(lambda0~1, sigma~1, phi~1), cjs.data,
                    start=list(lambda0=1.5, sigma=50, phi=0.5))
mod$fit()
mod
```

Back-transform
```{r}
#| label: cjs-mod-est
mod$get_par("lambda0", k = 1, j = 1)
mod$get_par("sigma", k = 1, j = 1)
mod$get_par("phi", k = 1, m=1)
```

# Spatial CJS with movement



## Modeling dispersal among years

What if activity centers move between years?
  
- Could affect estimates of detection parameters
- More importantly, might provide opportunity to study dispersal
  
  
Potential movement models}
    
- Random walk: ${\bm s}_t \sim \mbox{Normal}({\bm s}_{t-1}, \tau^2)$
- Random walk with attraction point: ${\bm s}_t \sim \mbox{Normal}({\bm  s}_{t-1} + \rho(\bar{\bm s} - {\bm s}_{t-1}), \tau^2)$
- Extensions can be made to allow for resource selection,
      landscape resistance, etc.^[https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ecy.3473]. 
  





## Simulating spatial CJS data with dispersal

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width='50%'}

Parameters and data dimensions
```{r}
#| label: move
T <- 10; K <- 5; n <- 25 ## same as before
phi <- 0.9; p0 <- 0.4; sigma <- 0.05
## dispersal parameter (of random walk)
tau <- 0.05
```

Activity centers take a random walk
```{r}
#| label: s
## state-space should be bigger
xlim <- ylim <- c(0, 1)
first <- rpois(n, 1)+1
s <- array(NA, c(n, 2, T))
for(i in 1:n) {
    s[i,,first[i]] <-
        cbind(runif(1, xlim[1], xlim[2]),
              runif(1, ylim[1], ylim[2]))
    for(t in (first[i]+1):T) {
        s[i,1,t] <- rnorm(1, s[i,1,t-1], tau)
        s[i,2,t] <- rnorm(1, s[i,2,t-1], tau)
    }
}
d <- p <- array(NA, c(n, J, T))
for(i in 1:n) {
    for(t in 1:T) {
        d[i,,t] <- sqrt((s[i,1,t]-x[,1])^2 +
                        (s[i,2,t]-x[,2])^2)
        p[i,,t] <- p0*exp(-d[i,,t]^2 /
                          (2*sigma^2))
    }
}
```
:::
    
::: {.column width='50%'}

Generate $z$ and $y$
```{r}
#| label: z3
z <- matrix(NA, n, T)
y.move <- array(NA, c(n, J, T)) 
for(i in 1:n) {
    z[i,first[i]] <- 1
    for(t in (first[i]+1):T) {
        z[i,t] <- rbinom(1, 1, z[i,t-1]*phi)
        for(j in 1:J) {
            y.move[i,j,t] <-
                rbinom(1, K, z[i,t]*p[i,j,t])
        }
    }
}
```
:::
:::



## Movement of activity center 1

```{r}
#| label: s1
#| out-width: "65%"
#| fig-align: "center"
plot(t(s[1,,]), pch=16, type="o", xlab="x", ylab="y",
     xlim=c(0, 1), ylim=c(0, 1), asp=1, col="blue")
points(x, pch=3)
```



## Movement of all activity centers

```{r}
#| label: s-all
#| out-width: "65%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| echo: false
par(mai=c(0.1,0.1,0.1,0.1))  
blue <- seq(0.1, 0.9, length=nrow(s))
plot(t(s[1,,]), pch=1, type="o", xaxt="n", yaxt="n", frame=FALSE, ann=FALSE,
     xlim=c(-0.2, 1.2), ylim=c(-0.2, 1.2), asp=1, col=rgb(0,0,blue[1],0.5))
for(i in 2:nrow(s)) lines(t(s[i,,]), pch=i, type="o", col=rgb(0,0,blue[i],0.5))
points(x, pch=3)
```


## Spatial CJS model with dispersal in JAGS
  
[CJS-spatial-move.jag](CJS-spatial-move.jag)
```{r}
#| label: jags-sp-move
#| background: 'beige'
#| comment: ''
#| echo: false
writeLines(readLines("CJS-spatial-move.jag"))
```



## JAGS
  
Data
```{r}
#| label: sp-move-data
jd.sp.move <- list(y=y.move, n=n, first=first, x=x,
                   J=J, K=K, T=T, xlim=xlim, ylim=ylim)
```
  Initial values for $z$, and parameters to monitor
```{r}
#| label: ji3
zi <- matrix(NA, n, T)
for(i in 1:n) {
    zi[i,(first[i]+1):T] <- 1
    }
ji.sp.move <- function() list(phi=runif(1), z=zi, s=s) ## Cheating with s
jp.sp.move <- c("phi", "p0", "sigma", "tau")
good1 <- which.max(rowSums(z, na.rm=TRUE)+rowSums(y.move, na.rm=TRUE))
time1 <- first[good1]:T
jp.s1x <- paste0("s[", good1, ",1,", time1, "]")
jp.s1y <- paste0("s[", good1, ",2,", time1, "]")
jp.z1 <- paste0("z[", good1, ",", time1, "]") 
```
  
Fit the model
```{r}
#| label: jc3
#| results: 'hide'
#| cache: true
jps.sp.move <- jags.basic(data=jd.sp.move,
                          inits=ji.sp.move,
                          parameters.to.save=
                              c(jp.sp.move, jp.s1x, jp.s1y, jp.z1),
                          model.file="CJS-spatial-move.jag",
                          n.chains=3, n.adapt=100, n.burnin=0,
                          n.iter=2000, parallel=TRUE)
```


## Posterior distributions
```{r}
#| label: jc3-plot
#| out-width: "60%"
#| fig-align: 'center'
plot(jps.sp.move[,jp.sp.move])
```


## Posterior movement path

```{r}
#| label: jc3-s
#| out-width: '80%'
#| fig-align: 'center'
#| echo: false
s1.post <- as.matrix(window(jps.sp.move[,c(jp.s1x,jp.s1y)], start=1501, thin=10))
z1.post <- as.matrix(window(jps.sp.move[,jp.z1], start=1501, thin=10))
plot(x, pch=3, xlim=c(0,1), ylim=c(0,1), asp=1, ann=FALSE)
for(i in 1:nrow(s1.post)) {
    alive1 <- which(z1.post[i,]==1)
    T1 <- length(alive1)
    arrows(s1.post[i,alive1[-T1]], s1.post[i,(alive1+T1)[-T1]],
           s1.post[i,alive1[-1]], s1.post[i,(alive1+T1)[-1]],
           col=rgb(0,0,1,0.1), length=0.05)
}
traps1 <- which(rowSums(y.move[good1,,], na.rm=TRUE)>0)
points(x[traps1,,drop=FALSE], pch=3, cex=2, lwd=2, col="red")
lines(t(s[good1,,]), type="o", pch=16, col="blue")
```




## Summary

Spatial CJS models allow for inference about survival, movement, and capture probability.

We could have considered many other movement models.

Next, we'll use Jolly-Seber models to study spatio-temporal variation in abundance and recruitment.
